about: The held-out coding session: every speed or quality claim made on the 59-turn Python-stdlib session (agent-60 shape, to 129k) is also reported on this one, so a change cannot be tuned to one text. Same rule as that session (BoltBeam's replay Words synthesis and shape draw), reimplemented for this document set, no gap draw: per turn new, tool and reply token counts drawn uniformly from the shape's ranges with its seed; the text is the document set read in path order by the model's own tokenizer (llama.cpp /tokenize of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GSQ-RCO IQ1_M, a CPU-only server), each turn taking the next slices: user = new + tool tokens, assistant = the next reply_tokens (a fixed recorded history: with --history recorded every arm sees byte-identical prompts). Different from the 59-turn session in language (Go, not Python), repository (golang/go, not CPython) and draw (seed 256, not 60). It stops before a turn would need more than 262,144 - margin_tokens tokens with headroom_tokens free. fits = the last turn that fits a context: play 1..fits[ctx] (session-ab --turns) on a server at that context. Reply lengths: each turn's reply_tokens (no --lengths file needed). Counts are the tokenizer's on the pieces; the server's chat template adds a few tokens per turn.

# Servers

ListenAndServe starts an HTTP server with a given address and handler.
The handler is usually nil, which means to use [DefaultServeMux].
[Handle] and [HandleFunc] add handlers to [DefaultServeMux]:

	http.Handle("/foo", fooHandler)

	http.HandleFunc("/bar", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		fmt.Fprintf(w, "Hello, %q", html.EscapeString(r.URL.Path))
	})

	log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))

More control over the server's behavior is available by creating a
custom Server:

	s := &http.Server{
		Addr:           ":8080",
		Handler:        myHandler,
		ReadTimeout:    10 * time.Second,
		WriteTimeout:   10 * time.Second,
		MaxHeaderBytes: 1 << 20,
	}
	log.Fatal(s.ListenAndServe())
